title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.1 Project Background
High-performance computing (HPC) is an important component of Australia’s research infrastructure, supporting computationally intensive research across a wide range of scientific fields (Australian Academy of Science 2024).
Australia has two national Tier-1 HPC facilities accessible to researchers: the National Computational Infrastructure (NCI) and the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre (National Computational Infrastructure, n.d.; Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre, n.d.).
As research becomes increasingly data- and compute-intensive, understanding how demand for HPC resources is changing is important for planning Australia’s future national research infrastructure (Australian Academy of Science 2024).

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.2 Project Purpose
The purpose of this project is to analyse historical Australian research computing demand and develop an evidence-based projection of future HPC demand to 2030 (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
The analysis is intended to support national policy discussions relating to public compute investment and future research infrastructure planning (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
The project combines data engineering, descriptive analysis and forecasting using publicly available NCI and Pawsey data, particularly information from the National Computational Merit Allocation Scheme (NCMAS), together with additional indicators where they are sufficiently consistent and relevant (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
Because historical reporting practices, hardware systems and compute accounting methods have changed over time, the analysis explicitly documents assumptions, derived values and limitations rather than treating all historical observations as directly comparable.

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.3 The Forecasting Problem
One of the main challenges in forecasting national research computing demand is that observed HPC allocation does not necessarily represent the full level of research demand.
National allocation schemes operate under finite capacity. As a result, allocated compute represents the amount of resource awarded rather than necessarily the amount researchers would use if additional capacity were available (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
Requested compute provides additional evidence of demand, but it may also understate underlying need where researchers constrain their requests based on expected availability or where potential users do not apply (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
The project therefore distinguishes between:

requested compute,
allocated compute,
the gap between requested and allocated compute, and
broader underlying or latent demand, which cannot be observed directly from the available allocation data.

A further challenge is that the historical series is not fully comparable across years. Reporting practices, hardware systems, compute units and service-unit accounting have changed over time, and CPU and GPU resources are not directly interchangeable (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
For this reason, the analysis uses the longest available historical series while explicitly documenting where values are directly reported, derived, estimated or based on assumptions. Forecasting results are therefore interpreted together with these data limitations rather than as precise measurements of unconstrained demand.

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.4 Project Objectives
The project aims to:

build a documented longitudinal dataset of Australian national HPC activity using publicly available NCI and Pawsey sources, including NCMAS allocation information,
document differences in reporting practices, compute units, systems and accounting methods across years,
improve comparability of historical compute measures where a defensible conversion or normalisation approach is available,
distinguish CPU and GPU resources where the available source data permits,
examine historical patterns in requested compute, allocation and oversubscription,
analyse changes in Field of Research composition using the most comparable available data,
assess potential indicators or structural drivers of research computing demand where suitable data are available,
develop and compare forecasting or projection approaches appropriate to the length and quality of the historical series, and
develop demand scenarios to 2030 and assess their implications for future national research computing requirements.

Throughout the analysis, assumptions, derived values, source limitations and uncertainty are documented explicitly.
The project objectives are informed by the internship brief, which emphasises longitudinal data assembly, descriptive analysis, structural demand modelling and scenario development (Australian Academy of Science 2026).

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.1 Purpose
The purpose of the data collection stage is to assemble a documented longitudinal evidence base for analysing Australian national research computing demand and allocation.
The project draws primarily on publicly available NCI, Pawsey and NCMAS reporting to identify historical requested compute, allocated compute, resource type, Field of Research and other available characteristics of national HPC allocations and usage (Australian Academy of Science 2026)
Additional datasets, including research funding, workforce and research activity indicators, are collected as potential structural drivers of future HPC demand where sufficiently consistent time-series data are available (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
Because the availability, scope and definition of variables differ substantially across years and sources, the purpose of this stage is not to assume that all collected observations are directly comparable. Instead, original values, units, reporting periods, source definitions and data limitations are retained so that their suitability for integration, standardisation and modelling can be assessed in subsequent stages.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.2 Data Sources
The project uses multiple public data sources from NCI, Pawsey and NCMAS, together with research funding, workforce and Field of Research datasets.
The specific HPC source varies by analytical year. Earlier observations are primarily drawn from annual reports, allocation documents and other historical NCI and Pawsey publications, while more recent observations increasingly use direct NCMAS outcome pages, applicant guidance and facility-specific allocation information.
In several years, different documents are used for different analytical components. Allocation outcomes, requested-demand information, resource availability and Field of Research composition may therefore originate from separate official publications.
For transparency and reproducibility, the exact source document, source location and URL are retained in the underlying yearly datasets. The principal sources used for each analytical year are summarised below.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.3 HPC Demand and Allocation Data
The main HPC dataset covers source periods from 2013/14 to 2025/26, corresponding to analytical years 2014 to 2026.
The collected information includes, where available:

requested compute,
allocated compute,
facility and computing system,
resource type,
original compute unit,
Field of Research,
institution,
allocation or reporting scope,
source document and URL, and
source reporting period.

The availability and level of detail of these variables vary substantially across years. Earlier observations are often available only as aggregate values reported in annual reports, while more recent NCMAS outcomes provide more detailed project-, facility- or resource-level information.
Requested and allocated compute are retained as distinct measures. Allocated compute represents resources awarded through the relevant allocation process, while requested compute provides additional evidence of demand where it is directly reported or can be defensibly derived.
Historical values are also retained in their original reported units before any conversion or standardisation is applied. This is important because service units, CPU hours, GPU hours and other compute measures are not directly interchangeable across facilities, systems or hardware generations (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
Where a value is not directly reported, its derivation or assumption is recorded separately so that directly reported, derived and proxy values can be distinguished during subsequent analysis.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.4 Field of Research Data
Field of Research (FoR) information was collected to examine how the disciplinary composition of national HPC allocations has changed over time.
The source, granularity and reliability of FoR information vary across years. Earlier observations are derived from annual reports, allocation summaries or project-level information with varying levels of detail, while more recent NCMAS outcomes provide more direct and consistent FoR information.
Where possible, reported FoR classifications are mapped to a common classification to support comparison across years. The original classification and source-reported FoR information are retained so that the standardisation process remains traceable.
The available FoR data primarily represents the composition of allocated compute rather than the composition of requested or latent demand. FoR allocation shares are therefore not interpreted directly as FoR-specific research demand.
Where allocation composition is subsequently combined with annual requested-compute totals to estimate demand by FoR, the resulting values are treated as analytical proxies rather than directly observed demand.
Because source scope and data quality differ across years, longer-term FoR trends are interpreted with caution, with the most confidence placed in years where direct and more comparable NCMAS FoR information is available.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.5 Potential Demand Drivers
Additional datasets are collected to investigate potential structural drivers of national research computing demand.
These include research funding, research workforce, research activity and related indicators that may help explain changes in HPC demand over time. The internship brief identifies competitive grant flows, research workforce size and changes in compute intensity as potential structural drivers of future demand (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
These variables are treated as candidate explanatory indicators rather than assumed drivers. Their suitability for modelling is assessed later based on historical coverage, consistency, temporal alignment and their observed relationship with the available HPC demand measures.
Variables with insufficient coverage or weak comparability are retained for contextual analysis where useful but are not necessarily included in the final forecasting model.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.6 Data Provenance
Data provenance is retained throughout the dataset so that each observation can be traced to its originating source information and, where relevant, the derivation used to construct it.
Where available, the retained provenance information includes:

source document or webpage,
source URL,
source reporting period,
source location or relevant section,
originally reported value and unit,
reporting or allocation scope, and
notes describing extraction, derivation or interpretation.

This information provides an audit trail for subsequent data integration, standardisation and conversion. It also makes it possible to distinguish values that are directly reported from those that are derived, estimated or based on analytical assumptions.
Maintaining provenance is particularly important because the historical HPC series is assembled from publications that differ in reporting format, scope, compute units and level of detail across years. Provenance information is therefore used to assess whether observations can be compared directly or require additional qualification before analysis.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.7 Data Collection Limitations
Several limitations were identified during the data collection stage.
The main limitations include:

limited availability of sufficiently consistent historical data before 2013,
requested compute may understate underlying demand where researchers constrain applications in response to expected resource availability,
changes in reporting formats, terminology and level of detail across years,
inconsistent availability of requested and allocated compute,
incomplete separation of CPU and GPU resources in some historical records,
changes in HPC systems, hardware generations and accounting methods,
differences in reporting scope between NCI, Pawsey and NCMAS sources,
changes in Field of Research classifications and reporting granularity, and
the use of derived or proxy values where directly reported measures are not available.

These limitations mean that the historical series cannot be treated as perfectly homogeneous or directly comparable across all years.
The impact of these issues is assessed in later stages of the project through data integration, standardisation, conversion and comparability assessment. Observations that require assumptions or additional qualification are retained with supporting provenance information rather than being treated as equivalent to directly reported values.

title: 3  Variable Definition
text:
3.1 Purpose
The purpose of the variable definition stage is to establish clear and consistent meanings for the measures used throughout the analysis.
The variables are organised into three main groups:
Not all defined variables are expected to enter the final forecasting model. Some are used primarily for descriptive analysis, comparability assessment or interpretation.
Variables considered for modelling are evaluated later based on their theoretical relevance, historical coverage, consistency of measurement, temporal alignment and suitability for the relatively short annual time series available.

title: 3  Variable Definition
text:
HPC demand variables, including requested compute and related demand indicators,

potential structural drivers that may help explain changes in research computing demand over time.

title: 3  Variable Definition
text:
3.2 HPC Demand
The main outcome of interest is Australian research demand for national HPC resources.
Demand is not directly observed through a single consistent measure. The internship brief notes that national HPC allocations are supply-constrained and that researchers may also limit requests based on expected availability, meaning that observed requests may not capture the full level of underlying need (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
The analysis therefore distinguishes between requested compute, allocated compute and underlying or latent demand.

3.2.1 Requested Compute
Requested compute represents the amount of HPC resource requested by researchers through an allocation process where this information is available.
It is treated as the primary observable indicator of research demand. However, requested compute may understate underlying need if researchers limit their requests based on expected resource availability or if potential users do not submit applications (Australian Academy of Science 2026).


3.2.2 Allocated Compute
Allocated compute represents the amount of HPC resource awarded to researchers through the relevant allocation process, as reported in NCMAS outcomes and related NCI and Pawsey allocation documentation (National Computational Merit Allocation Scheme 2024, 2025, 2026).
Allocation is analysed separately from demand because the amount awarded is constrained by available resources and the allocation process.


3.2.3 Latent Demand
Latent demand refers in this project to the broader level of HPC resources that researchers might require beyond what is observed in submitted requests or awarded allocations.
This is an analytical concept rather than a directly observed variable. The internship brief highlights that observed demand may be censored by available capacity and by researchers adapting their requests to expected resource availability (Australian Academy of Science 2026).

title: 3  Variable Definition
text:
3.3 Demand and Allocation Indicators
Several indicators are derived from the historical demand and allocation data to describe the relationship between requested and awarded compute.
The observed request-allocation gap is defined as:
\[
\text{Request-Allocation Gap}_t =
\text{Requested Compute}_t -
\text{Allocated Compute}_t
\]
A positive value indicates that reported requests exceeded the amount of compute allocated in year (t).
The fulfilment rate is defined as:
\[
\text{Fulfilment Rate}_t =
\frac{\text{Allocated Compute}_t}
{\text{Requested Compute}_t}
\]
A fulfilment rate below 1 indicates that allocated compute was lower than reported requested compute, while a value closer to 1 indicates that a larger proportion of reported requests was satisfied.
These indicators are used to describe allocation pressure over time. However, they are not interpreted as direct measures of total unmet research demand because requested compute may itself be constrained by expected resource availability and participation in the allocation process (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
The indicators are calculated only where requested and allocated compute refer to sufficiently comparable scope and resource definitions.

title: 3  Variable Definition
text:
3.4 Field of Research
Field of Research (FoR) variables are used to describe the disciplinary composition of national HPC allocation.
The principal FoR variables are:

for_classification: the standardised research field assigned to an observation,
allocation_share_for: the proportion of annual allocated compute associated with each FoR,
allocated_compute_for: allocated compute associated with each FoR, and
estimated_demand_by_for_proxy: an analytical estimate of requested compute by FoR where allocation composition is applied to annual requested compute.

The FoR allocation share for field (i) in year (t) is defined as:
\[
\text{Allocation Share}_{i,t}
=
\frac{\text{Allocated Compute}_{i,t}}
{\text{Total Allocated Compute}_{t}}
\]
Where allocation composition is applied to annual requested compute, the resulting FoR-level demand measure is explicitly treated as a proxy rather than directly observed demand.
This distinction is maintained because the available FoR information primarily describes allocation composition rather than the composition of submitted requests.

title: 3  Variable Definition
text:
3.5 Potential Structural Drivers
Potential structural drivers are candidate explanatory variables that may help describe changes in national HPC demand over time (Australian Academy of Science 2026).
They are not assumed to have a causal relationship with HPC demand and are considered for modelling only where historical coverage and measurement consistency are sufficient.

3.5.1 Research Funding
Research funding variables include available annual measures from:

Australian Research Council (ARC),
National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), and
Medical Research Future Fund (MRFF).

These variables are considered as indicators of changes in the scale of funded research activity that may be associated with research computing requirements.


3.5.2 Research Workforce and Activity
Research workforce and activity variables include available measures of:

research workforce size, and
research activity.

These variables are considered as indicators of changes in the scale of the Australian research system.


3.5.3 Compute Intensity
Compute-intensity indicators describe changes in the amount or type of computing associated with research activity.
Potential indicators include:

compute allocation per project,
compute allocation by Field of Research,
changes in CPU allocation, and
changes in GPU allocation.

These measures are used primarily to investigate whether the composition and intensity of research computing are changing over time.


3.5.4 HPC Infrastructure
HPC infrastructure variables describe changes in the supply environment within which observed demand and allocation occur.
Relevant variables may include:

computing system,
resource type,
available compute capacity, and
major system commissioning or retirement.

Infrastructure variables are interpreted separately from demand because an increase in allocated compute may reflect additional available capacity rather than an equivalent increase in underlying research demand.

title: 3  Variable Definition
text:
3.6 Variable Selection for Modelling
Not all variables defined in this chapter will be included in the final forecasting model.
Candidate variables will be assessed based on:

theoretical relevance to HPC demand,
historical data coverage,
consistency of measurement,
temporal alignment with the demand series,
observed relationship with the selected demand measure,
availability or defensible assumptions over the forecast horizon, and
the limited number of annual observations available for modelling.

Given the short annual time series, the final modelling approach will prioritise a small number of interpretable variables rather than a large set of predictors. Variables that are useful for descriptive analysis or interpretation may therefore be retained without being included in the final forecasting model.

title: 4  Data Integration
text:
4.1 Purpose
The purpose of the data integration stage is to combine the different datasets collected for the project into a structured analytical dataset while preserving their original values, units, scope and provenance.
The source datasets cover different reporting periods, levels of granularity and data structures. Integration is therefore required to align common identifiers such as analytical year, facility, computing system, resource type and Field of Research before the data can be analysed together.
At this stage, integration focuses on organising and linking the available information rather than forcing observations into common units or classifications. Differences in naming, classification and compute units are addressed subsequently through data standardisation and conversion.
Where datasets cannot be combined directly because of differences in scope or granularity, those distinctions are retained explicitly rather than assuming equivalence.

title: 4  Data Integration
text:
4.2 Main Datasets
The integration process combines several datasets covering 2014 - 2026, with different analytical roles.
The core HPC datasets include:

yearly HPC demand and allocation source workbooks,
Field of Research composition data, and
HPC system and capacity information.

Supporting datasets include:

research funding data, and
research workforce and research activity data.

The core datasets provide the historical evidence used to construct measures of requested compute, allocated compute and disciplinary composition. Supporting research funding, workforce and research activity datasets are retained separately for later integration into the modelling stage as candidate explanatory variables.
Because these datasets differ in temporal coverage, granularity and reporting scope, they are not merged indiscriminately. Integration is performed only where suitable common identifiers and compatible levels of aggregation are available.
Where annual demand or allocation measures are not directly available, derived or proxy values are constructed later from the integrated source evidence using explicitly documented assumptions. These selected annual measures are subsequently assembled into a separate summary dataset for modelling.

title: 4  Data Integration
text:
4.3 Yearly Source Integration
The detailed yearly source files are integrated before constructing the annual modelling summary.
For the HPC demand and allocation data, each yearly workbook contains multiple types of evidence. The integration therefore preserves the different analytical levels rather than reducing each workbook immediately to a single annual value.
Three recurring components are retained:

Project_Allocations, containing project or allocation-level records,
Context_Metrics, containing reported or derived annual and contextual measures, and
Resource_Envelope, containing information on available resources and system-level capacity.

Field of Research data are integrated separately from the yearly FoR_Composition sheets.
The source filename and source period are retained during integration so that each observation remains traceable to its original yearly workbook. The resulting integrated tables form the evidence base from which annual summary measures are selected or derived later.

4.3.1 Load Libraries and Define Paths


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

demand_path <- "assets/data/raw data/demand and allocation"
for_path <- "assets/data/raw data/field of research"

clean_path <- "assets/data/data clean"


The yearly demand and allocation workbooks are identified from the raw data directory.


Code
demand_files <- list.files(
  demand_path,
  pattern = "\\.xlsx$",
  full.names = TRUE
)


For the demand and allocation workbooks, the reporting period is derived from the source filename. A helper function is also defined to convert financial-year-style source periods to their ending analytical year.


Code
get_source_period <- function(path) {

  filename <- basename(path)

  years <- str_match(
    filename,
    "(\\d{4})_(\\d{2})"
  )

  paste0(
    years[, 2],
    "/",
    years[, 3]
  )
}

get_end_year <- function(source_period) {

  end_year <- str_extract(
    source_period,
    "(?<=/)\\d{2}$"
  )

  2000 + as.numeric(end_year)
}


Each yearly demand and allocation workbook contains several recurring worksheets. The same set of yearly workbooks is therefore used to extract each analytical component separately.

4.3.1.1 Integrate Context Metrics
Demand and allocation context metrics are combined across the yearly workbooks.
These records contain annual or supporting measures used to interpret requested compute, allocated compute and related demand-allocation relationships.


Code
context_metrics <- map_dfr(
  demand_files,
  function(file) {

    read_excel(
      file,
      sheet = "Context_Metrics",
      col_types = "text"
    ) |>
      mutate(
        source_file = basename(file),
        source_period = get_source_period(file)
      )
  }
)




4.3.1.2 Integrate Project Allocations
Project-level allocation records are combined across the yearly workbooks while preserving their original source-level structure.


Code
project_allocations <- map_dfr(
  demand_files,
  function(file) {

    read_excel(
      file,
      sheet = "Project_Allocations",
      col_types = "text"
    ) |>
      mutate(
        source_file = basename(file),
        source_period = get_source_period(file)
      )
  }
)




4.3.1.3 Integrate Resource Envelope
Resource-envelope records are combined across the yearly workbooks.
These records describe available HPC systems, resource availability and capacity-related information used to interpret the supply environment associated with observed demand and allocation.


Code
resource_envelope <- map_dfr(
  demand_files,
  function(file) {

    read_excel(
      file,
      sheet = "Resource_Envelope",
      col_types = "text"
    ) |>
      mutate(
        source_file = basename(file),
        source_period = get_source_period(file)
      )
  }
)




4.3.1.4 Align Analytical Year
A common analytical year is created to align observations across the different yearly source tables. The ending year of each source period is used as the common reference year where a consistent NCMAS or allocation year is not available.


Code

  mutate(
    year = get_end_year(source_period)
  )

project_allocations <- project_allocations |>
  mutate(
    year = coalesce(
      suppressWarnings(as.numeric(ncmas_year)),
      suppressWarnings(as.numeric(allocation_year)),
      get_end_year(source_period)
    )
  )

  mutate(
    year = coalesce(
      suppressWarnings(as.numeric(ncmas_year)),
      suppressWarnings(as.numeric(allocation_year)),
      get_end_year(source_period)
    )
  )

title: 4  Data Integration
section: 4.4 Annual Demand and Allocation Summary Construction
text:
4.4 Annual Demand and Allocation Summary Construction
The annual demand and allocation summary is constructed after integration of the detailed yearly source evidence.
The existing manually assembled summary is retained temporarily as a reference for reconciliation rather than treated as an independent source of data. Each annual requested and allocated compute value is checked against the integrated Context_Metrics, Project_Allocations and Resource_Envelope evidence.
Where a directly reported comparable annual value is available, that value is preferred. Where it is not available, a derived or proxy value may be constructed from the integrated evidence using an explicitly documented assumption.

4.4.1 Reconstruct Annual Demand and Allocation Summary
Annual demand and allocation measures are reconstructed from the integrated source tables before comparison with the previously assembled summary.
Context metrics are used to identify reported annual totals, ratios and derived demand information. Project-level allocations and resource envelopes are retained as supporting evidence and are aggregated only where their scope and units are sufficiently consistent.


Code
context_candidates <- context_metrics |>
  mutate(
    value_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value))
  ) |>
  filter(
    str_detect(
      metric,
      regex(
        "request|demand|allocat|fulfil|oversub|capacity|available",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    year,
    source_period,
    metric,
    value_num,
    unit,
    scope,
    source,
    notes
  ) |>
  arrange(year, metric)




Code
project_candidates <- project_allocations |>
  mutate(
    allocated_compute_num =
      suppressWarnings(as.numeric(allocated_compute))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(allocated_compute_num)) |>
  group_by(
    year,
    source_period,
    unit,
    allocation_type
  ) |>
  summarise(
    allocated_total = sum(allocated_compute_num),
    records = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(year, unit, allocation_type)




Code
resource_candidates <- resource_envelope |>
  mutate(
    resource_available_num =
      suppressWarnings(as.numeric(resource_available))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(resource_available_num)) |>
  group_by(
    year,
    source_period,
    unit
  ) |>
  summarise(
    resource_available_total =
      sum(resource_available_num),
    records = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(year, unit)




4.4.2 Construct Reconstructed Annual Summary
The annual series is reconstructed from the integrated evidence without using the previously assembled summary as an input.
Directly reported annual values are used where available. Derived values are calculated only where the required source values and relationships are contained in the integrated evidence. Where the integrated evidence is insufficient to reproduce an earlier summary value, the value is left missing for subsequent reconciliation rather than being inferred from the existing summary.


Code
get_metric_value <- function(target_year, metric_name) {

  values <- context_candidates |>
    filter(
      year == target_year,
      metric == metric_name
    ) |>
    pull(value_num)

  if (length(values) != 1) {
    stop(
      paste(
        "Expected one value for",
        target_year,
        metric_name,
        "but found",
        length(values)
      )
    )
  }

  values
}




Code
reconstructed_summary <- tibble(
  year = 2014:2026,
  source_period = paste0(
    year - 1,
    "/",
    str_sub(as.character(year), -2)
  )
) |>
  mutate(

    requested_compute = case_when(

      year == 2014 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2014,
          "ncmas_total_ksu_request"
        ),

      year == 2015 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2015,
          "nci_ncmas_implied_demand_2015"
        ),

      year == 2016 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2016,
          "nci_ncmas_implied_requested_compute_2016"
        ),

      year == 2017 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2017,
          "pawsey_ncmas_requested_compute_2017"
        ),

      year == 2018 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2018,
          "national_implied_requested_compute_2018"
        ),

      # Current integrated evidence does not contain the
      # 220 × 3 national proxy used previously.
      year == 2019 ~ NA_real_,

      year == 2020 ~
        resource_candidates |>
          filter(
            year == 2020,
            unit == "kSU"
          ) |>
          pull(resource_available_total) |>
          first() * 2,

      year == 2021 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2021,
          "direct_ncmas_2021_total_allocation"
        ) *
        get_metric_value(
          2021,
          "ncmas_demand_supply_factor_high"
        ),

      year == 2022 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2022,
          "ncmas_allocated_compute_total"
        ) /
        (
          get_metric_value(
            2022,
            "ncmas_allocated_share_of_requested_pct"
          ) / 100
        ),

      year == 2023 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2023,
          "ncmas_requested_compute"
        ),

      # Retrospective 57% and 56% demand relationships are
      # not currently retained in the integrated source tables.
      year == 2024 ~ NA_real_,
      year == 2025 ~ NA_real_,

      year == 2026 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2026,
          "ncmas_requested_compute"
        )
    ),

    allocated_compute = case_when(

      # 83,505 kSU is not currently retained as an annual
      # metric in the integrated evidence.
      year == 2014 ~ NA_real_,

      year == 2015 ~
        get_metric_value(

      year == 2016 ~

      year == 2020 ~
        get_metric_value(

      year == 2021 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2021,
          "direct_ncmas_2021_total_allocation"
        ),

      year == 2022 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2022,
          "ncmas_allocated_compute_total"
        ),

      year == 2023 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2023,
          "ncmas_allocated_compute_total"
        ),

      year == 2024 ~
        get_metric_value(
          2024,

        ),

      year == 2025 ~

        get_metric_value(2026, "ncmas_setonix_cpu_allocation") +

4.4.3 Compare Reconstructed and Existing Annual Summaries
The reconstructed annual series is compared with the previously assembled summary to identify values that are reproduced directly from the integrated evidence and values that require additional source evidence or documented derivation.

4.4.6 Final Reconciliation Check
After the missing annual measures are reconstructed and their basis is documented, the annual series is compared again with the previously assembled summary.

    old_requested = requested_compute,
    old_allocated = allocated_compute

    reconstructed_summary |>
      select(
        year,
        source_period,
        reconstructed_requested = requested_compute,
        reconstructed_allocated = allocated_compute,
        requested_basis,
        allocated_basis,
        derivation_note
      ),
    by = c("year", "source_period")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    requested_difference =
      reconstructed_requested - old_requested,

    allocated_difference =
      reconstructed_allocated - old_allocated,

    requested_match =

        old_requested,
        reconstructed_requested,

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to standardise the integrated historical High-Performance Computing (HPC) data to support consistent analysis across reporting years.
This stage uses the reconciled annual demand and allocation summary and the Field of Research (FoR) summary produced during Data Integration.
Standardisation focuses on aligning reporting periods, variable names, units, research field classifications, and data quality labels where necessary. Original values, source information, and derivation assumptions are retained to maintain traceability.
Numerical demand and allocation values are not converted at this stage. Compute-unit conversion is addressed separately in the Data Conversion chapter.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.2 Reporting Period
Reporting periods are standardised using the ending year of each annual reporting period. For example, 2013/14 is represented as 2014, and 2025/26 as 2026.
The analysis covers 13 annual observations from 2014 to 2026. The year column is retained as the analytical year, while source_period preserves the original reporting period.
Both variables are carried forward from Data Integration. This step validates their consistency without modifying the existing year assignments.

  mutate(
    expected_year = as.integer(
      sub("^.*[/\\-]", "", source_period)
    ) + 2000L

  filter(is.na(year) | year != expected_year)

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.3 Institution Names
Institution names may differ across historical sources because of abbreviations, naming conventions, or organisational changes.
The reconciled annual demand and allocation summary and Field of Research (FoR) summary do not contain institution-level observations. Therefore, no institution-name mapping is applied to these datasets.
Institution-level standardisation may be undertaken separately if institutional allocation data are included in subsequent analysis.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.5 HPC Facilities and Systems
Historical HPC demand and allocation data originate from Australia’s national computing facilities, including the National Computational Infrastructure (NCI) and Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.
The reconciled annual summary retains facility and system information within the original source descriptions. These include NCI allocation records, Pawsey historical reporting, and more recent NCMAS outcomes identifying Gadi and Setonix CPU and GPU resources separately.
Facility and system information is therefore available for some reporting periods, although it is not consistently represented in dedicated structured variables across the integrated annual dataset.
At this stage, the existing facility and system descriptions are retained without modifying the original records. Where system-level information is available, it will inform resource classification and conversion assumptions in the Data Conversion chapter.
Differences between NCI and Pawsey accounting conventions, system configurations, and CPU/GPU resource measures are preserved as comparability considerations. No assumption is made that allocations from different systems are directly equivalent.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.6 Resource Type
Historical HPC demand and allocation records include different computing resources, primarily CPU and GPU systems. The availability of resource-level information varies across reporting periods.
Earlier reporting years generally provide aggregate allocation or demand figures without a consistent CPU/GPU breakdown. Some historical systems, including Raijin and Magnus, are identified in the source records, but their system-level allocation shares are not always available.
More detailed resource-level information is available for later years. The 2020/21 allocation records identify Magnus, FlashLite, MASSIVE, and Gadi, while the 2021/22 records distinguish MASSIVE, Gadi, Setonix CPU, and Setonix GPU. From 2022/23 onwards, several reporting years provide separate Gadi CPU, Setonix CPU, and Setonix GPU allocations.
However, the availability of resource-level demand data is more limited. In particular, the 2023/24 and 2024/25 demand estimates are derived from aggregate allocation and fulfilment rates, without a directly reported CPU/GPU demand breakdown.
For standardisation, resource types are classified as CPU, GPU, or Unspecified only where supported by the original source information. Records without sufficient resource-level detail retain an unspecified classification rather than being assigned an estimated CPU/GPU split.
No numerical allocation or demand values are redistributed between resource types at this stage. Resource-specific conversion factors and comparability adjustments are addressed in the Data Conversion chapter.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.7 Units
The reconciled annual demand and allocation summary contains different computational accounting units across reporting periods.
The 2013/14 records are expressed in kSU. The 2014/15 and 2015/16 records contain mixed units, with demand expressed in million hours and allocation expressed in kSU. The 2016/17 records use million core-hours, while 2017/18 uses million hours and 2018/19 uses million CPU-hours.
From 2019/20 to 2025/26, annual demand and allocation values are recorded in kSU. However, the use of the same unit label does not necessarily establish equivalence between different HPC systems or CPU and GPU resources.
At the standardisation stage, original unit labels are retained without numerical conversion. Mixed-unit records are explicitly identified to prevent inappropriate direct comparisons.
The Data Conversion chapter will assess system-specific conversion factors, distinguish CPU and GPU accounting where supported, and document any assumptions required to establish comparable analytical measures.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.8 Data Quality and Comparability
The integrated historical HPC dataset combines directly reported demand and allocation figures with values derived from reported demand-to-supply relationships, fulfilment rates, and available computing capacity. Consequently, the quality and comparability of observations vary across reporting years.

5.8.1 Data Provenance and Estimation
Directly reported observations are retained as published in the original sources. Where demand figures are unavailable, existing estimates derived during Data Integration are preserved together with their calculation assumptions and source references.
For example, the 2014/15 and 2015/16 demand estimates are derived from reported demand-to-supply or fulfilment relationships. The 2017/18, 2020/21, 2023/24, and 2024/25 demand estimates similarly rely on reported allocation totals and demand-to-supply or fulfilment information.
The 2016/17 and 2018/19 records include capacity-based information or conservative demand proxies. These are distinguished from directly reported allocation and demand figures.
No demand estimates or allocation values are recalculated during Data Standardisation.


5.8.2 Comparability Across Reporting Years
Historical observations differ in their reporting scope, computational accounting units, and availability of system-level information.
In particular, the 2016/17 data include Pawsey-wide supercomputer usage and capacity information, which are not directly equivalent to NCMAS allocation outcomes in other years.
Differences between CPU and GPU resources, system-specific accounting conventions, and incomplete resource breakdowns also limit direct comparisons across reporting periods.
These limitations are retained in the analysis rather than resolved through unsupported assumptions.


5.8.3 Treatment for Subsequent Analysis
The standardisation process preserves original numerical values, source references, estimation assumptions, and existing data quality information.
Observations with different reporting scopes, derived demand values, or uncertain conversion assumptions will be explicitly considered during Data Conversion, exploratory analysis, and forecasting model evaluation.
Where appropriate, sensitivity analysis will be used to assess how historical proxies and comparability limitations affect the forecasting results.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.9 Output
The Data Standardisation stage prepares the reconciled historical HPC datasets for subsequent conversion, analysis, and forecasting.
Two datasets are carried forward:

Annual Demand and Allocation Summary: Retains the 13 annual observations from 2014 to 2026, including original demand and allocation values, reporting periods, accounting units, source references, and existing estimation information. No numerical conversions are performed at this stage.
Standardised Field of Research Summary: Retains the original FoR records and classification information while adding for_analysis_group for consistent historical reporting and visualisation.

The standardisation process preserves original numerical values, research field labels, source references, and estimation assumptions. Historical FoR categories are harmonised for reporting purposes without redistributing allocation shares.
Validation checks confirm reporting-period consistency, preservation of annual FoR allocation-share totals, and the absence of missing FoR reporting groups.
The resulting datasets provide the input for Data Conversion, where computational accounting units and system-specific conversion assumptions will be evaluated before numerical comparisons and forecasting are undertaken.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to convert historical High-Performance Computing (HPC) demand and allocation values into more comparable computational resource measures across reporting years, facilities, and systems.
The integrated dataset covers 13 financial years, from 2013/14 to 2025/26, and contains observations reported in different accounting units, including kilo service units (kSU), million compute hours, CPU core-hours, and GPU-related service units.
These observations originate from different HPC facilities and systems, including the National Computational Infrastructure (NCI) and Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre. Historical system information includes Raijin, Magnus, FlashLite, MASSIVE, Gadi, and Setonix CPU and GPU resources.
Service-unit accounting conventions can vary across facilities, systems, resource types, and reporting periods. Consequently, values expressed in the same unit, such as kSU, are not necessarily computationally equivalent.
This stage therefore evaluates conversion rules at the system and resource level rather than applying a single conversion factor across the historical dataset.
Where sufficient documentation is available, original demand and allocation values are converted into CPU core-hours or GPU hours using the applicable accounting rules. Where conversion cannot be supported reliably, original values and their limitations are retained without introducing unsupported assumptions.
The conversion process preserves the original reported values, units, source references, derivation methods, and conversion assumptions to maintain transparency and reproducibility for subsequent exploratory analysis and forecasting.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.2 Conversion Approach
The conversion process uses the standardised annual demand and allocation dataset produced in Chapter 04, together with the system-level resource information collected during Data Integration.
Each historical observation is assessed according to its reporting period, facility, HPC system, resource type, original accounting unit, and available conversion documentation.
The conversion process follows four principles:

Preserve original observations. Original demand and allocation values, units, source references, and derivation assumptions are retained without modification.
Identify resource-specific information. CPU and GPU resources are distinguished where supported by the original source records. Aggregate observations without a documented resource split remain unallocated to a specific resource type.
Apply documented conversion rules. Conversion factors are selected according to the relevant system, resource type, and reporting period. No universal service-unit-to-compute-hour factor is assumed.
Record conversion uncertainty. Where direct conversion rules or resource-level observations are unavailable, transparent assumptions are applied to produce estimated values. Each assumption is documented with its rationale, supporting evidence, confidence level, and limitations. Reported, derived, and assumed values remain distinguishable throughout the analysis.

The general relationship between kilo service units (kSU) and service units (SU) is:
\[
\text{SU} = \text{kSU} \times 1000
\]
However, conversion from service units to physical computational hours depends on the accounting rules of the relevant HPC system.
For example, CPU core-hours and GPU hours require separate conversion factors and cannot be combined directly into a single physical compute-hour measure.
The conversion framework therefore maintains separate demand and allocation measures and records conversion status, supporting evidence, and limitations for each observation.
Where system-level breakdowns are available, they will be assessed separately before aggregation. Historical observations lacking sufficient detail will not be assigned unsupported CPU/GPU proportions.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.3 CPU Resources
CPU resource conversion translates historical service-unit allocations and reported compute hours into CPU core-hours.
The conversion is performed at the HPC system level where sufficient information is available. This is necessary because the accounting relationship between service units and CPU core-hours may differ across facilities and reporting periods.
For observations reported in kSU, CPU core-hours are calculated as:
\[
\text{CPU core-hours} =
\frac{\text{CPU kSU} \times 1000}
{\text{SU per CPU core-hour}}
\]
For observations already reported in CPU core-hours, the original values are retained without applying an additional service-unit conversion.
Where aggregate kSU values include both CPU and GPU resources, the CPU component must first be identified or estimated before the conversion formula is applied.
The conversion framework considers the historical systems identified during Data Integration, including Raijin, Magnus, FlashLite, MASSIVE, Gadi, and Setonix CPU.
Documented accounting factors are prioritised. Where system-specific factors or resource splits are unavailable, assumptions are applied with explicit justification, source references, and confidence classifications.
All calculations preserve the original observations and distinguish directly reported CPU values from derived and assumed estimates.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.4 GPU Resources
GPU resource conversion translates GPU-specific service-unit allocations and demand into GPU-hours.
Unlike CPU core-hours, GPU-hours represent the use of GPU resources and depend on the accounting conventions of the relevant HPC system.
For GPU observations reported in kSU, the conversion is:
\[
\text{GPU hours} =
\frac{\text{GPU kSU} \times 1000}
{\text{SU per GPU hour}}
\]
The analysis prioritises directly reported GPU demand and allocation figures. Where GPU demand is unavailable, estimates are developed using documented assumptions and available resource-level evidence.
The conversion distinguishes reported GPU observations from estimated values. Historical years without a documented GPU breakdown require separate assessment rather than being automatically classified as having zero GPU demand.
Original source values, conversion factors, assumptions and limitations are preserved for reproducibility.

6.5 Field of Research Conversion
The Field of Research (FoR) conversion estimates the distribution of computational resources across research disciplines using the standardised FoR allocation dataset from Chapter 04.
The conversion uses each field’s annual allocation share to distribute the corresponding annual CPU core-hours and GPU-hours. This assumes that the resource composition within each field is proportional to the overall annual allocation composition.
The resulting FoR-level CPU and GPU values are estimates rather than directly observed resource-specific allocations. Original FoR observations and classification variables are retained to support traceability and subsequent analysis.
The 2016/17 reporting period requires particular caution because the available FoR information reflects Pawsey-wide reporting rather than the same NCMAS allocation scope used in other years. This difference will be explicitly flagged.
Before conversion, the FoR allocation shares are checked for completeness and consistency within each reporting year.

)

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.6 Output
The Data Conversion stage produces three reproducible datasets for subsequent analysis and forecasting.
The annual converted dataset contains 13 financial years of HPC demand and allocation observations, including converted CPU core-hours and GPU-hours. Original reported values, source references, and conversion assumptions are retained.
The Field of Research converted dataset contains 133 observations with estimated allocations in kSU, CPU core-hours, and GPU-hours, distributed according to the standardised annual FoR allocation shares. These resource-specific field estimates are based on proportional allocation assumptions rather than directly observed CPU or GPU usage.
A separate historical GPU scenario dataset preserves low, baseline, and high estimates for 2013/14 – 2020/21 to support sensitivity analysis.
All converted datasets are stored separately from the standardised source datasets. Reconciliation checks confirm that the FoR allocations reproduce annual resource totals within numerical tolerance.
Historical conversion factors, estimated resource shares, differences in reporting scope, and assumptions regarding CPU/GPU composition remain important limitations for interpretation and forecasting.

title: 7  Initial Analysis
text:
7.1 Purpose
The purpose of this stage is to examine historical demand and allocation patterns for Australian national High-Performance Computing (HPC) resources from 2014 to 2026, using the converted datasets produced in Chapter 05.
The analysis focuses on identifying trends in computational resource demand, allocation levels, and potential differences between requested and allocated resources. CPU core-hours and GPU-hours are examined separately because they represent distinct computational resource types and cannot be directly combined.
The analysis also examines the distribution of HPC allocations across Fields of Research (FoR) to identify how allocated computational resources are distributed among research disciplines and how these patterns have changed over time.
Particular attention is given to historical reporting differences, conversion assumptions, and estimated resource values. These limitations are considered when interpreting trends and assessing the suitability of the data for forecasting.
The findings from this stage will inform subsequent forecasting model development, evaluation, and scenario analysis through 2030.

Historical HPC demand and allocation are examined across the 2014 - 2026 analytical period to identify changes in requested computational resources, awarded allocations, and the difference between them.
Requested compute is used as an indicator of researcher demand, while allocated compute reflects the resources awarded within available infrastructure and programme constraints. These measures are therefore interpreted separately.
The analysis uses the converted annual kSU series to examine demand and allocation trends, annual growth rates, request allocation gaps, and fulfilment rates. However, historical values include directly reported observations, derived estimates, and capacity-based proxies. Consequently, observed changes may partly reflect reporting differences or changes in infrastructure rather than underlying demand alone.

7.2.4 Initial Findings
The annual HPC demand and allocation series show an overall upward trend between 2014 and 2026. Reported or estimated demand increases from approximately 131,356 kSU in 2014 to 2,242,817 kSU in 2026, while allocation increases from approximately 83,505 kSU to 872,288 kSU.
Demand exceeds allocation in every analytical year. The largest absolute gap occurs in 2026, when demand exceeds allocation by approximately 1.37 million kSU. The corresponding fulfilment rate is approximately 38.9%, compared with 56.0% in 2025.
The series also exhibits periods of substantial change, particularly around 2018, 2021, and 2026. However, these changes should not automatically be interpreted as equivalent increases in underlying researcher demand. Historical conversion assumptions, differences in reporting scope, capacity-based allocation proxies, and changes in HPC systems may contribute to the observed variation.
These findings suggest a persistent difference between requested and allocated computational resources. Further analysis of CPU and GPU resources is required to understand whether similar patterns are present across distinct computational resource types.

7.2.4.1 Interpretation of the 2026 Demand Increase
The marked increase in reported demand in 2026 requires particular caution. It is not yet established whether this represents a sustained increase in underlying researcher demand, a temporary change, or an effect of reporting scope and conversion assumptions. Following expert statistical feedback, subsequent forecasting will examine the sensitivity of trend estimates to the inclusion of 2026 and compare simple linear and log-linear models.

7.3 CPU and GPU Resources

The analysis uses the converted CPU core-hours and GPU-hours produced in Chapter 05. These measures provide resource-specific perspectives on HPC demand and allocation, although their interpretation remains subject to system-level accounting conventions and historical conversion assumptions.

7.3.3 Initial Findings
The resource-specific analysis indicates an overall increase in estimated CPU and GPU demand between 2014 and 2026, although the two series exhibit different patterns and levels of uncertainty.
CPU Resources
Estimated CPU demand increases from approximately 130.0 million CPU core-hours in 2014 to 1,235.0 million CPU core-hours in 2026. Over the same period, CPU allocation increases from approximately 82.7 million to 518.6 million CPU core-hours.
CPU demand remains above allocation throughout the analytical period. Substantial fluctuations are visible around 2018 – 2022, followed by a sustained increase in estimated demand from 2022 to 2026. In contrast, CPU allocation remains relatively stable between 2023 and 2026, at approximately 491 – 528 million CPU core-hours.
The widening difference between CPU demand and allocation in recent years suggests increasing pressure on allocated CPU resources. However, the magnitude of historical changes should be interpreted cautiously because earlier observations include assumed conversion factors, capacity proxies, and estimated CPU/GPU resource shares.
GPU Resources
Estimated GPU demand increases from approximately 0.04 million GPU-hours in 2014 to 3.00 million GPU-hours in 2026. GPU allocation increases from approximately 0.02 million to 1.25 million GPU-hours over the same period.
The GPU series shows a pronounced increase between 2021 and 2022, followed by fluctuations in estimated demand and comparatively stable allocations during 2022–2026. By 2026, estimated GPU demand is approximately 2.4 times the allocated GPU-hours.
However, the historical GPU series requires particular caution. Values for 2014–2021 are based on assumed GPU resource shares and a provisional conversion factor rather than directly observed GPU demand and allocation. The low, baseline, and high scenarios demonstrate that historical GPU estimates are sensitive to these assumptions.
Furthermore, GPU allocation from 2022 onward is derived from reported system-level service units using a working conversion factor, while GPU demand includes both directly reported and estimated values. The apparent increase around 2022 may therefore partly reflect changes in reporting coverage, infrastructure, and conversion methodology rather than an equivalent increase in underlying GPU demand.
Implications for Forecasting
The CPU and GPU series suggest different historical demand patterns and should be considered separately during forecasting model development. The observed differences between demand and allocation also reinforce the importance of distinguishing researcher demand from computational resources awarded under capacity constraints.
Historical uncertainty, system transitions, and the limited availability of directly observed GPU demand should be considered when selecting modelling periods and evaluating forecast reliability. Scenario analysis will be particularly important for assessing the sensitivity of GPU forecasts to historical conversion assumptions.

The analysis examines allocation composition rather than directly observed researcher demand. FoR-specific kSU, CPU core-hours and GPU-hours are derived using allocation shares and should not be interpreted as independently measured resource consumption by each discipline.
The 2017 observation is interpreted cautiously because its Pawsey-wide reporting scope differs from the other observations. Other source and classification limitations also affect longitudinal comparability.

7.4.5 Field of Research Reporting Periods
The 2014–2020 and 2021–2026 periods are examined separately to assess differences in research-field allocation composition.

Physical Sciences and Chemical Sciences are retained separately in both periods. Combined categories are used where necessary to improve visual consistency, without modifying the original classifications.
Allocation shares represent the distribution of allocated HPC resources, not directly observed researcher demand. The 2017 FoR data have a different Pawsey-wide reporting scope and should be interpreted cautiously.

7.4.6.4 Implications for HPC Demand Forecasting
The historical FoR analysis provides evidence about the disciplinary composition of allocated HPC resources. It may help identify research areas relevant to future capacity planning and provide context for forecast scenarios.
However, three limitations must be considered:

Allocation shares represent the distribution of available resources, not directly observed unmet researcher demand.
Changes in research-field classification and reporting scope limit direct comparability across all years.
FoR-specific CPU and GPU resource measures are proportionally allocated estimates, rather than directly observed resource consumption by discipline.

Accordingly, the FoR results should primarily inform the interpretation of aggregate demand forecasts and the development of disciplinary scenarios. They should not be used as independent discipline-level demand forecasts without additional evidence.

title: 8  Forecasting Models
text:
8.1 Purpose
This chapter aims to develop transparent, reproducible, and statistically defensible forecasting models to estimate Australian national research supercomputing demand through 2030.
Building on the harmonised historical dataset and initial findings presented in Chapters 03 - 06, the analysis evaluates alternative approaches for modelling annual researcher demand, expressed in CPU-equivalent core-hours.
The modelling framework has four objectives:
Following expert statistical feedback, particular emphasis is placed on model simplicity, transparent assumptions, and the limitations of extrapolating trends from a relatively short and heterogeneous historical dataset.
The forecasts are intended to provide evidence-informed planning scenarios rather than precise predictions of future researcher demand.

title: 8  Forecasting Models
text:
Establish a suitable historical demand series for forecasting, accounting for data quality, reporting differences, and conversion assumptions.
Develop and compare candidate forecasting models, prioritising simple and interpretable approaches such as linear and log-linear trends.
Examine the sensitivity of projected demand to the substantial increase observed in 2026, distinguishing potential structural changes from temporary fluctuations.
Generate alternative demand projections for 2027 - 2030 to support national HPC infrastructure planning and policy discussions.

title: 8  Forecasting Models
text:
8.2 Forecast Target and Data Suitability

8.2.1 Forecast Target
The forecasting analysis considers three related but distinct measures of Australian national research supercomputing demand:

Overall HPC demand, expressed in thousands of service units (kSU).
CPU demand, expressed in CPU core-hours.
GPU demand, expressed in GPU-hours.

These measures represent harmonised estimates of computing resources requested by researchers, rather than allocated resources or available computing capacity. CPU and GPU demand are modelled separately because their resource units and conversion assumptions are not directly interchangeable.
The overall kSU series provides a reference for aggregate demand, while the CPU and GPU series support resource-specific forecasts relevant to future infrastructure planning.


8.2.2 Historical Data Suitability
The historical demand series provides a consistent analytical unit for forecasting, but it should not be interpreted as a fully homogeneous set of directly observed demand measurements.
Depending on the year and reporting source, historical estimates include directly reported demand, derived estimates, and proxy-based measures. Differences in facility coverage, reporting definitions, and CPU/GPU conversion assumptions introduce uncertainty into comparisons across years.
The relatively small number of annual observations also limits the complexity of forecasting models that can be estimated reliably. Consequently, simple trend-based models will be prioritised, while more flexible time-series approaches will be used as benchmarks.
The substantial increase in reported demand in 2026 presents an additional uncertainty. Available historical observations do not establish whether this increase represents a sustained shift in researcher demand, a temporary fluctuation, or a difference in measurement or reporting scope.
Accordingly, the modelling analysis will consider both the complete historical series (2014–2026) and a sensitivity specification excluding 2026 (2014–2025). The latter is not treated as a more accurate historical dataset, but as a means of assessing how strongly the latest observation influences projected demand.


8.2.3 Forecasting Horizon
The forecasting horizon covers four annual periods:

2027
2028
2029
2030

Forecasts will be reported in the original units of each target: kSU for overall HPC demand, CPU core-hours for CPU demand, and GPU-hours for GPU demand.
The GPU analysis will explicitly distinguish historical scenario-based estimates from later reported or derived values, rather than treating all historical GPU observations as equally reliable.
The resulting forecasts are conditional projections based on historical patterns and modelling assumptions. They should not be interpreted as precise estimates of future HPC requirements, particularly given uncertainty surrounding emerging GPU-intensive workloads, changes in research activity, and future infrastructure investment.

8.3 Data Preparation and Validation
The forecasting analysis uses the converted annual demand and allocation dataset produced in Chapter 05. The dataset is loaded directly from its saved RDS file to ensure that this chapter can be executed independently of the preceding analysis.
The preparation process retains the historical demand observations without modifying their original values. Validation checks confirm the expected annual coverage, uniqueness of observations, and availability of positive demand values.

8.4 Candidate Forecasting Models

8.4.1 Overall HPC Demand: Linear and Log-Linear Trends
Two initial trend models are fitted to the harmonised annual HPC demand series for 2014–2026.
The linear trend models demand directly in kSU, assuming a constant absolute change over time. The log-linear trend models the natural logarithm of demand, allowing for approximately constant proportional growth.
Both specifications are retained for subsequent evaluation. Neither is assumed to be the preferred model before out-of-sample validation.

title: 8  Forecasting Models
text:
8.5 Sensitivity Analysis: Influence of 2026
The substantial increase in reported HPC demand in 2026 introduces uncertainty into the estimation of future demand trends.
To assess the influence of this observation, the linear and log-linear trend models are refitted using historical observations from 2014 - 2025. These results are compared with the corresponding models fitted to the complete 2014–2026 dataset.
This analysis does not assume that the 2026 observation is incorrect or should be excluded from the final forecasting model. Instead, it evaluates how sensitive the estimated trend is to the inclusion of the latest observation.

8.5.1 Trend Sensitivity Comparison


Code
# Historical data excluding 2026
overall_pre2026_data <- overall_model_data |>
  dplyr::filter(year <= 2025)

# Refit the same model specifications

  demand_ksu ~ time,
  data = overall_pre2026_data
)

overall_loglinear_pre2026 <- lm(
  log(demand_ksu) ~ time,
  data = overall_pre2026_data
)

# Compare trend coefficients
trend_sensitivity <- data.frame(
  model = c("Linear trend", "Log-linear trend"),
  full_2014_2026 = c(
    coef(overall_linear)[["time"]],
    coef(overall_loglinear)[["time"]]
  ),
  excluding_2026 = c(
    coef(overall_linear_pre2026)[["time"]],
    coef(overall_loglinear_pre2026)[["time"]]
  )
)

trend_sensitivity$percentage_change <- with(
  trend_sensitivity,
  100 * (full_2014_2026 - excluding_2026) /
    abs(excluding_2026)
)

The comparison evaluates changes in the estimated annual trend coefficients. For the linear model, the coefficient represents the annual absolute change in demand measured in kSU. For the log-linear model, the coefficient represents the annual change in log demand, which can be converted into an implied compounded growth rate.
Changes in these coefficients indicate how strongly the latest observation influences the fitted historical trend. They do not, on their own, establish whether the 2026 increase represents a structural change in underlying researcher demand.


8.5.2 Sensitivity Analysis Findings
Including the 2026 observation increases the estimated linear trend from approximately 144,357 to 161,992 kSU per year, representing a 12.2% increase in the annual absolute growth coefficient.
In contrast, the log-linear trend coefficient decreases slightly when 2026 is included, from approximately 0.239 to 0.233, equivalent to a reduction of approximately 2.4% in the estimated log-scale trend coefficient.
These results indicate that the latest observation has a greater relative influence on the estimated absolute growth rate than on the proportional growth trend.
Nevertheless, the relatively small change in the log-linear coefficient does not necessarily imply that its future forecasts are insensitive to 2026, since changes in the fitted intercept may also influence projected demand levels.
The analysis therefore supports retaining both model specifications for further evaluation. It does not establish whether the 2026 increase represents a temporary fluctuation or a sustained change in researcher demand.

Differences between the fitted coefficients indicate the sensitivity of estimated historical CPU demand trends to the latest observation. They do not establish whether changes in 2026 are temporary or structural, nor do they determine which model has superior


8.6.4 CPU Sensitivity Findings
Including the 2026 observation increases the estimated linear CPU demand trend from approximately 72.41 to 81.01 million core-hours per year, representing an increase of 11.9% in the annual absolute growth coefficient.
In contrast, the log-linear trend coefficient changes only slightly, decreasing by approximately 0.4% when 2026 is included.
These results suggest that the 2026 observation has a greater relative influence on the estimated absolute CPU demand growth rate than on the proportional growth trend.
However, the limited change in the log-linear coefficient does not necessarily imply that projected CPU demand is insensitive to 2026, as changes in the fitted intercept may also affect future forecasts.
The sensitivity analysis does not establish whether the 2026 increase represents a sustained change in underlying researcher demand or reflects temporary conditions, reporting differences, or conversion assumptions.
Both linear and log-linear CPU models are therefore retained for subsequent forecast evaluation in Chapter 08.

title: 8  Forecasting Models
text:
8.7 GPU Demand Forecasting Models
GPU demand is analysed separately from overall HPC and CPU demand because GPU-hours represent a distinct resource measure with different conversion assumptions and reporting characteristics.
The harmonised GPU demand series covers 2014 - 2026. However, the historical observations are not equally suitable for forecasting.
For 2014 - 2021, GPU demand values were constructed using hypothetical conversion scenarios rather than directly reported GPU demand. These estimates are useful for exploring historical resource requirements but should not be treated as independently observed GPU demand.
For 2022 - 2026, the dataset contains a combination of reported and derived GPU demand estimates. Consequently, the later observations provide a more relevant basis for preliminary GPU forecasting, although they remain subject to reporting and conversion uncertainty.
Given these limitations, the initial GPU modelling analysis will focus on 2022–2026. Any fitted trends will be interpreted as exploratory scenarios rather than reliable estimates of long-term GPU demand growth.

8.7.1 GPU Data Provenance and Modelling Period


Code
# Retain GPU demand and its methodological metadata

  dplyr::transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    gpu_million_hours = as.numeric(demand_gpu_hours) / 1e6,
    gpu_demand_method = gpu_demand_method,
    gpu_demand_confidence = gpu_demand_confidence
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

# Define the later historical period for exploratory modelling

  dplyr::filter(year >= 2022, year <= 2026) |>
  dplyr::mutate(time = year - 2022)

# Validate recent GPU demand values

  identical(gpu_recent_data$year, 2022:2026),
  all(is.finite(gpu_recent_data$gpu_million_hours)),
  all(gpu_recent_data$gpu_million_hours > 0)
)

8.7.2 GPU Linear and Log-Linear Trends

The linear trend model estimates an annual increase in GPU demand of approximately 0.172 million GPU-hours over 2022–2026.
The log-linear model estimates an implied compounded annual growth rate of approximately 8.5%. However, neither trend coefficient is statistically significant at the 5% level.

8.7.4 GPU Demand Sensitivity Analysis
The sensitivity of GPU demand trends to the 2026 observation is examined by comparing models fitted over 2022–2026 with equivalent models fitted over 2022 - 2025.
This analysis is particularly important because the recent GPU demand series contains only five annual estimates, combining reported Setonix-based demand with values derived using GPU allocation shares and conversion assumptions.
Excluding 2026 reduces the modelling sample to four observations. The resulting comparison is therefore exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence of a structural change or as a reliable basis for selecting the preferred forecasting model.

Including the 2026 observation increases the estimated linear GPU demand trend from approximately 0.012 to 0.172 million GPU-hours per year, representing a relative increase of approximately 1,330.8% in the trend coefficient.

title: 8  Forecasting Models
text:
8.8 Historical GPU Conversion Scenario Assessment
The historical GPU conversion scenarios developed in Chapter 05 provide an indication of how assumptions about service-unit conversion affect estimated GPU resource requirements.
For 2014 - 2021, the low, baseline, and high GPU-hour series are hypothetical conversion scenarios rather than independently observed GPU demand. They should therefore not be treated as additional historical observations or automatically included in the recent-period GPU forecasting models.
The baseline scenario uses an assumed conversion of 36 service units per GPU-hour. Alternative conversion assumptions generate different GPU-hour estimates from the same underlying service-unit quantities.
These scenarios represent measurement and conversion uncertainty, rather than evidence of alternative historical demand growth patterns.

8.8.1 Historical Scenario Consistency

  "assets/data/data converted/historical_gpu_scenarios.rds"
)

    sort(as.numeric(historical_gpu_scenarios$year)),
    as.numeric(2014:2021)
