section: 8.10 Field of Research Demand Modelling Framework
text:
8.10 Field of Research Demand Modelling Framework

8.10.1 Purpose and Modelling Approach
Field of Research (FoR) demand is considered as an additional dimension of national HPC planning, complementing the overall HPC, CPU, and GPU demand projections developed in this chapter.
Unlike the aggregate and resource-specific demand measures, the harmonised FoR dataset primarily describes the distribution of allocated computing resources across research fields.
Consequently, FoR-specific demand cannot be treated as independently observed researcher demand.
A top-down allocation-share approach is therefore proposed to estimate indicative FoR-level demand through 2030.
Under this approach, the selected overall HPC demand forecast will be distributed across harmonised FoR groups using explicit assumptions about their future allocation shares.
The modelling relationship is:
\[
\widehat{D}_{f,t} = \widehat{D}_{t} \times s_{f,t}
\]
where:

\(\widehat{D}_{f,t}\) represents indicative demand for FoR group \(f\) in year \(t\), expressed in kSU.
\(\widehat{D}_{t}\) represents the selected overall HPC demand forecast in year \(t\), expressed in kSU.
\(s_{f,t}\) represents the assumed allocation share of FoR group \(f\) in year \(t\).

The assumed shares will be constrained to be non-negative and sum to one within each forecast year, ensuring that the indicative FoR demand estimates reconcile with the overall HPC demand projection.


8.10.2 Historical FoR Data Suitability
The historical FoR analysis in Chapter 06 covers 2014 - 2026 and includes changes in research classification standards, reporting coverage, and analytical grouping.
The earlier period (2014 - 2020) is primarily organised using FoR 2008 classifications, while the later period (2021 - 2026) uses FoR 2020 classifications.
Although Chapter 06 harmonised these classifications into broader analytical groups for visualisation, the resulting categories are not perfectly equivalent across periods.
Furthermore, allocation shares reflect the distribution of computing resources awarded to research fields, rather than the full amount of computing resources requested by researchers.
For these reasons, historical FoR allocation shares will be treated as indicators of research activity composition rather than direct measures of FoR demand.


8.10.3 FoR Allocation-Share Scenarios
Three approaches will be considered for developing future FoR allocation-share assumptions:

Recent composition: hold the latest available harmonised FoR allocation shares constant through 2030.
Recent-period average: use average allocation shares from the FoR 2020 reporting period (2021 - 2026).
Composition-change sensitivity: examine how alternative share assumptions affect indicative demand across broad research fields.

These approaches are proposed modelling assumptions, not statistically validated predictions of future research-field composition.
The suitability of the historical shares and their variation across recent years will be assessed in Chapter 08.
Final assumptions will be selected in Chapter 09, and indicative FoR demand scenarios for 2027 - 2030 will be generated in Chapter 10.


8.10.4 Interpretation and Limitations
The resulting FoR projections will represent indicative distributions of overall forecast HPC demand under specified allocation-share assumptions.
They should not be interpreted as independently forecast researcher requests by FoR, nor as evidence that historical allocation shares fully capture unmet computing demand.
Differences in FoR classification, facility coverage, and allocation practices may affect the comparability of historical shares.
The top-down approach preserves consistency with the selected overall HPC demand projection while making the underlying assumptions transparent.
These limitations will be retained when interpreting FoR-specific planning implications.

title: 8  Forecasting Models
text:
8.11 Modelling Summary and Limitations

8.11.1 Summary of Candidate Demand Projections
This chapter developed linear and log-linear forecasting models for three quantitative measures of Australian national research supercomputing demand: overall HPC demand in kSU, CPU demand in core-hours, and GPU demand in GPU-hours.
In addition, a top-down allocation-share framework was established to develop indicative Field of Research (FoR) demand scenarios. Unlike the three quantitative forecasting targets, FoR-specific demand is not independently modelled from observed researcher requests.
The models were fitted using harmonised historical estimates, with alternative specifications excluding 2026 to assess the influence of the latest observation.

8.11.2 Key Modelling Findings
The overall HPC and CPU analyses identify substantial historical demand growth. However, projected demand through 2030 differs considerably between linear and log-linear specifications, particularly because compounded proportional growth produces increasingly divergent trajectories.
For overall HPC and CPU demand, excluding 2026 increases or decreases projected demand depending on the model specification. The estimated log-linear growth coefficients are comparatively stable, although changes in fitted intercepts can still affect future projections.
GPU demand exhibits substantially greater uncertainty. The exploratory models use only five annual estimates from 2022 - 2026, combining reported Setonix-based demand with allocation-share-derived estimates.
Both GPU trend specifications are sensitive to the inclusion of 2026, and neither provides strong statistical evidence of a stable historical growth pattern. Consequently, GPU projections should be interpreted as exploratory trajectories rather than reliable long-term forecasts.
For Field of Research, the proposed modelling approach distributes the selected overall HPC demand forecast across harmonised research fields using explicit allocation-share assumptions. This approach preserves consistency with aggregate demand projections while recognising that historical FoR allocation shares do not directly measure researcher demand. The resulting FoR projections will be developed as indicative planning scenarios rather than independently estimated demand forecasts.


8.11.3 Limitations and Implications for Forecast Evaluation
Several limitations affect the interpretation of the candidate projections.
First, the historical demand series combines directly reported, derived, and proxy-based estimates, with differences in reporting coverage and conversion assumptions.
Second, the overall HPC and CPU models are fitted to only 13 annual observations, limiting the reliability of complex forecasting approaches and long-horizon extrapolation.
Third, the historical GPU conversion scenarios for 2014 - 2021 represent hypothetical estimates rather than independently observed demand. They are retained as evidence of conversion uncertainty but are not included in the recent-period GPU trend models.
Fourth, the substantial increase in reported demand in 2026 has not been established as a sustained structural change. Its influence is therefore examined through alternative model specifications rather than assumed to persist.
Fifth, the FoR modelling framework relies on historical allocation shares rather than directly observed research-field demand. Changes in FoR classification standards, reporting coverage, and allocation practices limit historical comparability. Consequently, FoR-level projections will depend on explicit assumptions about future research-field composition.
Finally, the candidate models have not yet been selected using out-of-sample predictive accuracy. In-sample fit statistics alone are insufficient for identifying the most defensible forecasting approach.
Chapter 08 will evaluate the overall HPC, CPU, and GPU candidate models using time-series cross-validation, consistent forecast error measures, and residual diagnostics where appropriate.
It will also examine the stability and comparability of historical FoR allocation shares to inform the development of FoR-specific planning scenarios.
The resulting evidence will support model selection in Chapter 09 and the development of national HPC demand scenarios through 2030 in Chapter 10.

9.2 Evaluation Framework

9.2.1 Candidate Models and Benchmarks
The evaluation considers four forecasting approaches:

Naïve benchmark: forecasts future demand using the most recent available observation.
Drift benchmark: extrapolates the average annual change between the first and most recent observations in the training sample.
Linear trend: estimates a constant annual absolute change in demand.
Log-linear trend: estimates approximately constant proportional growth using a regression model fitted to log-transformed demand.

Naïve and drift forecasts provide simple reference points against which the regression-based models can be evaluated.
The linear and log-linear specifications follow the modelling framework established in Chapter 07, including sensitivity analyses excluding the 2026 observation.
More complex models will not be prioritised unless their additional complexity can be justified by the available data and demonstrated predictive performance.


9.2.2 Time-Series Cross-Validation
Forecast accuracy will be assessed using rolling-origin time-series cross-validation.
At each evaluation origin, models will be estimated using only observations available up to that year. Forecasts will then be compared with subsequent historical observations.
This approach preserves chronological ordering and avoids using future observations to estimate models evaluated on earlier periods.
One-step-ahead evaluation will provide the primary comparison because the historical series are relatively short.
Where sufficient observations are available, additional forecast horizons may be examined to assess the stability of longer-term extrapolations.
The evaluation will distinguish between the longer overall HPC and CPU series covering 2014–2026 and the shorter GPU modelling series covering 2022 - 2026.
For GPU demand, the small number of recent observations severely limits the number of meaningful cross-validation origins. Any accuracy comparisons will therefore be considered exploratory.


9.2.3 Forecast Accuracy Measures
Forecast errors will be evaluated on the original scale of each demand measure using:

Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), which gives greater weight to larger forecast errors.
Mean Absolute Error (MAE), which measures the average absolute forecast error.

Accuracy measures will be calculated separately for overall HPC, CPU, and GPU demand because their units are different.
For log-linear models, predictions will be back-transformed to the original demand scale before calculating forecast errors. The evaluation will distinguish exponentiated log-scale predictions from bias-adjusted mean forecasts where relevant.
Models will be compared using common evaluation origins within each demand measure to ensure a fair comparison.


9.2.4 Model Selection Principles
The preferred forecasting approach will not be selected solely on the basis of the lowest numerical error.
Model selection will also consider:

Stability across evaluation periods and forecast origins.
Sensitivity to the inclusion of the 2026 observation.
Residual behaviour and evidence of systematic model errors.
Interpretability and consistency with historical data provenance.
The risks of extrapolating growth patterns through 2030.

Particular caution will be applied to GPU demand because its historical modelling period is short and includes estimates derived from different reporting and conversion methods.
The evaluation results presented in this chapter will provide the statistical evidence for model selection in Chapter 09 and the development of demand scenarios in Chapter 10.

9.3 Rolling-Origin Cross-Validation

9.3.1 Overall HPC Demand: One-Step-Ahead Evaluation
The initial evaluation focuses on overall HPC demand, measured in thousands of service units (kSU).
Rolling-origin cross-validation is applied using an initial training period of 2014 - 2020. At each subsequent origin, the training sample expands by one year, and a one-step-ahead forecast is generated for the following year.
This produces six evaluation years, from 2021 to 2026.
Four forecasting approaches are evaluated using identical training periods and forecast origins:

Naïve benchmark.
Drift benchmark.
Linear trend.
Log-linear trend.

Each model is re-estimated using only the observations available at the corresponding forecast origin. This avoids information leakage from future observations.


Code
# Load harmonised annual demand data
annual_converted <- readRDS(
  "assets/data/data converted/annual_demand_allocation_converted.rds"
)

# Prepare overall HPC demand series
overall_cv_data <- annual_converted |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    demand_ksu = as.numeric(demand_ksu)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

# Validate historical series
stopifnot(
  identical(overall_cv_data$year, 2014:2026),
  all(is.finite(overall_cv_data$demand_ksu)),
  all(overall_cv_data$demand_ksu > 0)
)

# Define common one-step-ahead evaluation years
cv_test_years <- 2021:2026

# Generate forecasts using expanding training windows
overall_cv_predictions <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(cv_test_years, function(test_year) {

    training <- overall_cv_data |>
      dplyr::filter(year < test_year) |>
      dplyr::mutate(time = year - 2014)

    actual <- overall_cv_data$demand_ksu[
      overall_cv_data$year == test_year
    ]

    future <- data.frame(time = test_year - 2014)

    # Naïve: last observed demand
    naive_forecast <- tail(training$demand_ksu, 1)

    # Drift: average change from first to last observation
    drift_forecast <- tail(training$demand_ksu, 1) +
      (
        tail(training$demand_ksu, 1) -
          training$demand_ksu[1]
      ) / (nrow(training) - 1)

    # Linear trend fitted only to training data
    linear_fit <- lm(
      demand_ksu ~ time,
      data = training
    )

    linear_forecast <- as.numeric(
      predict(linear_fit, newdata = future)
    )

    # Log-linear trend fitted only to training data
    loglinear_fit <- lm(
      log(demand_ksu) ~ time,
      data = training
    )

    loglinear_forecast <- exp(as.numeric(
      predict(loglinear_fit, newdata = future)
    ))

    data.frame(
      year = test_year,
      actual = actual,
      naive = naive_forecast,
      drift = drift_forecast,
      linear = linear_forecast,
      loglinear = loglinear_forecast
    )
  })
)

Rolling-origin one-step-ahead cross-validation over 2021–2026 indicates that the linear trend model achieves the lowest forecast errors among the four evaluated approaches.

text:
9.4 Field of Research Allocation-Share Evaluation

9.4.1 Purpose and Evaluation Approach
The Field of Research (FoR) evaluation examines the historical distribution and stability of HPC resource allocations across research fields.
Unlike the overall HPC, CPU, and GPU evaluations, this analysis does not assess independently observed FoR-specific researcher demand forecasts.
Instead, it evaluates whether historical allocation shares provide a sufficiently consistent basis for developing indicative FoR demand scenarios through 2030.
The analysis focuses on 2021–2026, corresponding to the FoR 2020 classification period used in Chapter 06.
Three considerations guide the evaluation:

Historical stability of FoR allocation shares.
Variation between the latest-year composition and the recent-period average.
Sensitivity to classification, reporting coverage, and allocation-based measurement assumptions.

The results will inform the selection of FoR share assumptions in Chapter 09 and their application to overall HPC demand forecasts in Chapter 10.

Two reporting periods are considered:

The full historical period (2014 - 2026), using broad harmonised analytical groups to examine long-term allocation composition.
The recent period (2021–2026), using FoR 2020-based analytical groups to evaluate recent allocation-share stability.

The full-period analysis provides historical context, while the recent-period analysis informs the assumptions used for indicative FoR demand scenarios.

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to use the selected modelling approach to forecast Australian research HPC demand to 2030 under different scenarios.
The scenarios are designed to represent different possible developments in Australian research activity and compute intensity rather than producing a single estimate of future demand.
The resulting demand forecasts are then compared with available or projected national HPC capacity to identify potential capacity gaps.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.2 Forecast Horizon
The selected modelling approach is used to produce forecasts to 2030.
Forecast uncertainty is reported where appropriate to reflect the uncertainty associated with both the historical data and future assumptions.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.3 Scenario Framework
Three main scenarios are considered:

Status quo
Restored national R&D intensity
AI acceleration

Each scenario uses the same overall modelling framework but applies different assumptions about the future development of relevant demand drivers.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.4 Status Quo Scenario
The status quo scenario represents a continuation of current research and HPC demand conditions.
Future values of the structural drivers are based on recent trends or other reasonable baseline assumptions.
This scenario provides a baseline against which the alternative scenarios can be compared.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.5 Restored National R&D Intensity Scenario
This scenario considers higher research activity associated with an increase in Australia’s research and development intensity.
Changes in relevant drivers, such as research funding and research activity, are translated into future HPC demand using the selected modelling approach.
The assumptions used for this scenario are documented explicitly.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.6 AI Acceleration Scenario
The AI acceleration scenario considers stronger growth in compute-intensive research associated with increasing use of artificial intelligence, machine learning and accelerated computing.
Particular attention is given to GPU demand because these workloads may have different resource requirements from traditional CPU-based research computing.
The scenario assumptions are based on available evidence and are documented separately from the historical observations.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.7 CPU and GPU Forecasts
Where supported by the available data, CPU and GPU demand are forecast separately.
This avoids assuming that CPU core-hours and GPU hours are directly interchangeable and allows differences in their future growth to be examined.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.8 Capacity Comparison
Forecast demand is compared with available or projected national HPC capacity where suitable capacity information is available.
Demand and capacity are only compared where their units and definitions are sufficiently consistent.
The general capacity-gap calculation is:
\[
\text{Capacity Gap}_t =
\text{Forecast Demand}_t -
\text{Available Capacity}_t
\]
A positive value indicates forecast demand above the capacity represented in the comparison.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.9 Facility-Equivalent Capacity
Where sufficient information is available, the estimated capacity gap may also be expressed in facility-equivalent terms.
This provides a more interpretable indication of the scale of additional computing infrastructure that may be required.
Any facility-equivalent calculation depends on assumptions about system capacity, resource type and utilisation. These assumptions are therefore reported explicitly.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.10 Scenario Comparison
The three scenarios are compared to examine how different assumptions affect projected HPC demand to 2030.
The comparison focuses on:

total forecast demand
CPU demand
GPU demand
growth relative to the historical period
estimated capacity gaps
differences between scenarios
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.11 Uncertainty and Sensitivity
Scenario forecasts are not treated as precise predictions of future HPC demand.
Results depend on the selected model, historical data, conversion assumptions and future values assumed for the structural drivers.
Sensitivity analysis is used where appropriate to examine how changes in key assumptions affect the forecast results.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.12 Policy Interpretation
The scenario results are interpreted in the context of Australia’s future national research computing requirements.
The analysis focuses on the potential scale and composition of future demand and the implications of different research and technology trajectories for national HPC infrastructure.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.13 Output
The output of this step is a set of scenario forecasts to 2030 together with estimates of potential capacity gaps.
These results provide the main quantitative evidence used in the final technical report, policy summary and project presentation.

12.2 AI Acknowledgement
Generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, were used to support aspects of this project such as brainstorming, reviewing code, improving written expression, and assisting with the organisation of the analysis and documentation.
All data preparation, analytical decisions, model development, interpretation of results, and final conclusions were reviewed and verified by the author.
